(p-393) Surat al-Anbiya' (The Prophets). It has one hundred and twelve verses according to the Kufan count, and one hundred and eleven according to the Madinan and Basran counts.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near to them, while they are heedless and turning away.﴾ [﴿Iqtaraba﴾ means "drew near" (dana). The lam in ﴿lil-nas﴾ is a complementary particle (silah) attached to iqtaraba.] It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that by "mankind" (al-nas) are meant the polytheists, because what follows describes the attributes of the polytheists. ﴿Their reckoning﴾ is the time of Allah's calling them to account and recompensing them for their deeds, that is, the Day of Resurrection. He described it as having "drawn near" because what remains is little compared with what has passed, and because everything that is coming is near. ﴿And they are in heedlessness﴾ of their reckoning and of what will be done to them; ﴿turning away﴾ from preparing for that Day. The drawing near is general, while heedlessness and turning away vary according to the varying states of the responsible persons. Some are heedless of their reckoning because they are absorbed in their worldly life and turn away from their Master; and some are heedless of their reckoning because they are consumed in their Master and turn away from their worldly life, so such a person does not awaken except by seeing his Master, whereas the former only awakens in the army of the dead. So it is obligatory upon you to take account of yourself before you are called to account, to be alert to the Reckoning before you are alerted, to turn away from the heedless, and to occupy yourself with the remembrance of the Creator of all creatures, so that you may succeed in meeting the Lord of the worlds.

﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord﴾ [meaning] a portion of the Qur'an, ﴿newly revealed﴾ in the sending down. Its being established is recent, its recitation is of recent occurrence, and the time of their hearing it is close. What is meant by it is the arranged letters (al-huruf al-manzumah), and there is no disagreement about their being originated (huduth, i.e., having come into existence in time). ﴿But they listen to it﴾ from the Prophet (ﷺ) or from another who recites it, ﴿while they play﴾, mocking it.

(p-394)

﴿heedless﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a state clause) referring to the pronoun in yalʿabūna (﴿they play﴾), or it is a clause introduced by wa-hum (﴿while they are playing﴾). Heedless and [the ḥāl] are two ḥāls referring to the pronoun in istamaʿūhu (﴿they listened to it﴾). Whoever reads lāhiyatun with a ḥamma (marfūʿ, nominative) makes it a khabar (predicate) following another khabar, relating to the word wa-hum. ﴿their hearts﴾ is raised (marfūʿ) by lāhiyatan (﴿heedless﴾). It derives from "lahā ʿanhu," when one forgets and becomes inattentive. The meaning is: their hearts are inattentive to what they are being addressed with. From this, Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the heedless heart is the one preoccupied with the adornment and splendour of this world and unmindful of the Hereafter and its terrors. ﴿and they concealed﴾ and exaggerated in hiding ﴿the secret counsel﴾, which is a noun derived from tanājī (private conferring). Then ﴿who did wrong﴾ is substituted (badal) for the wāw of wa-asarrū, to signal that they are the ones marked by wrongdoing in what they concealed. Alternatively, it follows the dialect of the one who said ʾakalūnī al-barāghīthu (﴿the fleas ate me﴾), where the wāw is treated as a plural subject marker. Or it is majrūr in its position (maḥall majrūr) by being a ṣifah (adjective) or a badal (substitute) for al-nās (﴿the people﴾). Or it is manṣūb in its position (maḥall manṣūb) as a dhamm (expression of censure). Or it is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar is asarrū al-najwā (﴿they concealed the secret counsel﴾), placed before it, meaning: and those who did wrong concealed the secret counsel. ﴿Is this not but a human like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?﴾ All of this statement is in a naṣb (accusative) position as a badal of "the secret counsel," meaning: and they concealed this speech. It is also permissible for it to be linked to a hidden qālū (﴿they said﴾). The meaning is that they believed the Messenger could only be an angel, and that anyone from among humans who claims prophethood and brings a miracle is a sorcerer, and his miracle is magic. Therefore they said, in denial: Will you then come to magic while you witness and see clearly that it is magic?

"Said (my Lord)" — Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafs read it as "qāla rabbī," meaning: Muḥammad said it; the others read "qul rabbī," meaning: say, O Muḥammad, to those who held secret counsel: ﴿He knows the word in the heaven and the earth﴾, that is: He knows the speech of every speaker who is in the heaven and the earth, whether secret or open. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what is in their hearts.

Al-Nasafi, Madarik al-Tanzil, on surah 21, verse 5:

﴿Nay, they say: "They are confused dreams. Nay, he has invented it. Nay, he is a poet."﴾ They turned away from their saying that it is magic, to saying that it is a confusion of dreams which he saw in his sleep, so he imagined them to be revelation from Allah to him. Then they turned to saying that it is a fabricated speech of his own. Then they turned to saying that it is the word of a poet. Thus is falsehood: it wavers, and the one who adheres to falsehood keeps reverting, not steady in his saying, one consistent position. Then they said: "If he is truthful in his claim, and the matter is not as he supposes, then let him bring us a sign" (﴿فَلْيَأْتِنا بِآيَةٍ﴾), meaning a miracle, ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾, meaning as those before him were sent, with the white hand and the staff, the healing of the blind and the raising of the dead. The comparison in their saying "as the earlier ones were sent" is correct in that it carries the sense of "as the earlier ones brought signs," because the sending of messengers entails bringing signs. Do you not see that there is no difference between your saying "Muhammad was sent" and your saying "Muhammad brought a miracle"? So Allah answered their saying with His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 6:

﴿Not one town that We destroyed before them believed.﴾ "From the people of a town" (min ahl qaryatin): ﴿We destroyed﴾ (ahlaknāhā) is a description of "a town" (qaryah) at the time the proposed signs came, because they had asked for them out of obstinacy. ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ That is: those (earlier people) did not believe in the signs when they came to them, so will these proposers believe if We brought them what they proposed, even though they are more defiant than those? The meaning is: the people of the destroyed towns proposed signs to their prophets and pledged that they would believe when they appeared, but when they came to them they broke their word and opposed (them), so Allah destroyed them. Therefore, if We gave these people what they propose, they would break their word as well.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 7:

﴿And We did not send before you except men⦆ This is the answer to their saying ﴿Is this except a human being like you?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 3]. ﴿To whom We revealed⦆ [Yusuf: 109] "Nuhi" (We reveal) is read by Hafs. ﴿So ask the people of the reminder⦆ the scholars of the two Scriptures (ahl al-kitabayn), for they know that the messengers to whom revelation was sent were humans and were not angels. The people of Makkah used to rely on their word ﴿if you do not know⦆ that. Then He clarified, like those who preceded him among the prophets, by His saying (p-396)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 8:

﴿And We did not make them a body﴾ — He made "body" singular because the intended sense is the kind (jins). ﴿That do not eat food﴾ — this is a qualifier of "body," meaning: We did not make the prophets before him beings with a body that do not eat (i.e., beings with a body that were not eaters of food). ﴿Nor were they immortal﴾ — as if they had said: "Why was he not an angel who is not fed and is made eternal?" — either believing that the angels do not die, or calling their extended survival and prolonged life "immortality" (khulud).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 9:

﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them﴾ by saving them. The original form is "fulfilled the promise to them" (ṣadaqnāhumu al-waʿd), with the object placed in the accusative after the verb, as in ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning: from among his people. ﴿So We saved them﴾ from what befell their people, ﴿and whom We willed﴾ are the believers, ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾, those who exceeded the limit through disbelief. The statement that the transgressors were destroyed indicates that "whom We willed" refers to others than them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 10:

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you﴾ O assembly of Quraysh, ﴿a Book in which is your reminder﴾: your honour, if you act upon it; or because it is in your tongue; or in it is your admonition; or in it is mention of your religion and your worldly affairs. And the clause, i.e., "in it is your reminder," is a description (ṣifah) of "a Book." ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ what We have favoured you with over others, so that you would believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 11:

﴿وَكَمْ﴾ (How many) is in the accusative, governed by his statement ﴿قَصَمْنا﴾ (We destroyed), i.e., We annihilated ﴿مِن قَرْيَةٍ﴾ (a town), i.e., its people, as indicated by His statement ﴿كانَتْ ظالِمَةً﴾ (which was wrongdoing), meaning disbelieving. It is used of severe anger and great wrath, because al-qasm (breaking, shattering) is the most dreadful kind of breaking, namely the breaking that separates the parts so that their joining is made evident, unlike al-fasm (splitting), which is a breaking without separation. ﴿وَأنْشَأْنا﴾ (And We brought into being), i.e., We created, ﴿بَعْدَها قَوْمًا آخَرِينَ﴾ (after them another people), so they dwelt in their dwellings.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 12:

﴿When they sensed Our might﴾, i.e., those who were destroyed. ﴿Our might﴾ means Our punishment; that is, they came to know it by sensory perception and direct witnessing. ﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it﴾, from the town. Here "idha" (behold, suddenly) indicates the sudden occurrence (li-l-mufaja'ah), and "hum" (they) is the subject (mubtada'), while the predicate is ﴿fleeing﴾, i.e., running away in haste. Al-rakd (fleeing in haste) is striking the animal with the leg (to spur it on). It is permissible that they mounted their animals and spurred them while fleeing from their town when the vanguard of the punishment overtook them. Or they were likened, in the speed of their running on foot, to riders spurring their mounts. Then it was said to them: (p-397)

"Do not flee (ارْكُضُوا) ..." — translation follows.

Do not gallop away, and the one speaking is some of the angels: "Do not flee [lit. do not gallop away], and return to what you were made to enjoy therein," that is, you were given comfort and soft living in the world. Al-Khalil said: al-mutraf is one whose life has been made wide and abundant, and whose concern in it is little. "And to your dwellings, that perhaps you may be questioned," meaning: it is said to them, mockingly at them, "Return to your luxury and your dwellings, that perhaps you will be questioned tomorrow about what befell you and what came down upon your wealth, so that you may answer the questioner with knowledge and eyewitness." Or it means: sit as you were in your sitting-places until your servants and those whose command and prohibition you carry out ask you, and they say to you, "What do you command? And how shall we come and go?" as is the custom of pampered people who are served. Or people will ask you in your assemblies, those who help in the calamities of misfortunes; or the visitors and the greedy who come to you will ask you, seeking the rain of your palms. Some of them also said to one another, "Do not flee and return," to your homes and your wealth, that perhaps you may be asked for property and tribute, so that you will not be killed. Then it was called out from the sky: "O vengeance of the prophets!" and the swords took them, and there [they were].
﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ Their acknowledgment of that when acknowledgment will no longer benefit them.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 15:

﴿So that cry of theirs did not cease﴾ "That" (تِلْكَ) is a reference to "Alas for us!" (يا ويْلَنا). "Cry" (دَعْواهُم) means their calling out (دُعاءَهم). "That" (تِلْكَ) is in the nominative case, as the subject of "ceased" (زالَتْ), and "their cry" (دَعْواهُمُ) is the predicate, meaning "the cry." It is also permissible to reverse this, making "their cry" the subject and "that" the predicate.

﴿until We made them a harvest﴾ "Like the harvest" (مِثْلَ الحَصِيدِ), that is, like cut crops (الزَرْعِ المَحْصُودِ). "Harvest" (حَصِيدًا) is not made plural, just as "the one who is decreed" (المُقَدَّرُ) is not made plural.

﴿extinguished﴾ "Dead" (مَيِّتِينَ), like the extinguishing of a fire (خُمُودَ النارِ). "Harvest" (حَصِيدًا) and "extinguished" (خامِدِينَ) are the second object of "made" (جَعَلَ), meaning: We made them ones who combine the likeness of the harvest and the extinguishing, just as you say "I made it sweet, sour," meaning: I made it combine the two tastes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 16:

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ Al-La'ib (play): an action that pleases at first but has no permanence to it. La'ibin (playing) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of ﴿khalaqna﴾ (We created). The meaning: We did not make this raised canopy and this spread-out bed, and what is between them of kinds of creation, for amusement and play. Rather, We made them so that they may serve as evidence for the power of their Governor, and so that We may recompense the doer of good and the doer of evil according to what Our wisdom requires. (p-398)

Then He declared His essence free from the marks of createdness by His saying ﴿If We had wished to take a diversion﴾, i.e., a son or a wife, as if He were refuting those who said, "Jesus is His son, and Mary is His consort." ﴿We would surely have taken it from Our presence﴾, from among the youths or the maidens of paradise (al-hur). ﴿If We were doing [it]﴾, i.e., if We were among those who do such a thing, and We are not among those who do it, since it is impossible for Us. It has also been said that this is a negation, like His saying ﴿And I do not know﴾ [al-Anbiya': 109], i.e., We were not doing [it].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 18:

﴿Nay, We hurl﴾ Bal (بَلْ): a turning away (idrab) from taking up amusement, and a declaration that God is exalted above it in His essence, as if He had said: "Glory be to Us that We should take up amusement. Rather, it is Our custom to hurl," i.e., to cast down and impose, ﴿the truth﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿against falsehood﴾, that is, Satan; or the truth as Islam against polytheism; or seriousness against play; ﴿and it crushes it﴾, i.e., breaks it, and the truth overcomes falsehood. This is a subtle metaphor (isti'arah latifah), because the original use of "qadhf" (hurling) and "damgh" (crushing) is for physical bodies. Then "qadhf" was borrowed for bringing the truth down upon falsehood, and "damgh" for eliminating falsehood. So the borrowed-from (al-musta'ar minhu) is sensory (hissi) and the borrowed-for (al-musta'ar lahu) is intellectual ('aqli). It is as if it were said: "Rather, We launch the truth, likened to a strong body, against falsehood, likened to a weak body, and it annihilates it, as a strong body annihilates a weak one." ﴿Then behold, it﴾, i.e., the falsehood, ﴿vanishes﴾, perishes and departs. ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾, namely, what you attribute to God of offspring and the like.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 19:

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, in creation and in ownership. So how could any part of them be a child of His, when between the two there is contradiction? One may pause on "the earth" (al-ard), because ﴿and those who are with Him﴾ refers to rank and high standing, not to a place or location. It means: the angels. [The phrase] is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿they do not disdain﴾, meaning they do not consider themselves great, ﴿from His worship, nor do they tire﴾, meaning they do not grow weary.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

The phrase ﴿لا يَفْتُرُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject of ﴿يُسَبِّحُونَ﴾ (the subject of the verb "they glorify"). That is, their glorification is continuous and constant at all times; no interval of leisure or of some other occupation interrupts it. Their glorification proceeds just as breathing proceeds with us.

(p-399)

Then He turns away from the polytheists, denouncing and rebuking them. So He brings in am (أم), which carries the meaning of bal (بل, "rather") together with the interrogative hamza, and says: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead?﴾ That is, who bring the dead to life. The phrase "from the earth" (مِنَ الأرْضِ) is a qualifier of "gods" (آلهة), because their gods were made of earthly substances such as gold, silver and stone, and they were worshipped on earth. So they are attributed to it, like your saying "So-and-so is from the city," meaning "he is a city-dweller" (madani). Alternatively, it is connected to "have taken" (اتخذوا), and in that case it specifies the extent of the taking.

In His words ﴿who raise the dead﴾ there is an added rebuke. Even though they did not claim that their idols bring the dead to life, and how could they claim it, since among the greatest impossibilities is that the dead should raise some of the dead, it nevertheless follows from ascribing divinity to them that they claim the power of raising the dead, because one incapable of it cannot validly be a god, for this name deserves only the one who is capable of every possible thing, and raising the dead is among the possible things.

Al-Hasan (al-Basri) read yunshirun (يَنْشُرُونَ) with a fatha on the ya', and both are dialectal forms: anshara Allah al-mawta and nasharaha, meaning He brought them to life.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 22:

﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah﴾. That is: other than Allah. "Gods" is qualified by "illa" (except) just as it would be qualified by "ghayr" (other than) if one said "gods other than Allah." It is not permissible to read it in the nominative as a substitute (badal), because "law" (if) has the same status as "inna" (indeed) in that the speech following it is affirmative (mujab), and substitution is only valid in non-affirmative speech, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And none of you shall look back, except your wife﴾ [Hud: 81]. Nor is it permissible to read it in the accusative as an exception (istithna'), because when a plural noun is indefinite, it is not permissible, according to the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqin), to make an exception from it, since it has no generality (umum) that would include the excepted item were it not for the exception. The meaning is: if there were gods managing the affairs of the heavens and the earth, diverse and other than the One who originated them both, ﴿they would have been ruined﴾, that is, laid waste, because of the existence of mutual opposition (tamanu'). We have established this in the principles of kalam (usul al-kalam). Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying, ﴿Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe﴾, namely, of offspring and partners.

He is not questioned about what He does, because He is the true Owner. Even if some of His servants were to object to a sovereign's act, despite their being of the same kind, the possibility of error on their part, and the absence of true ownership on their part, that would be considered ugly and deemed foolishness. So how much more fitting is it that He, the King of kings and Lord of lords, whose every act is right, should not be objected to. "But they will be questioned": because they are owned and prone to error, so how fitting it is that they be told, "Why did you do that?" for every act they committed. It was also said that "they will be questioned" refers to the Messiah and the angels, meaning: they are answerable, so how could they be gods, when divinity contradicts being of a like kind and being answerable?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 24:

﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ The repetition (al-i'ada) is for the sake of added benefit. The first (denial) is on the basis of reason (al-'aql), and the second on the basis of transmitted revelation (al-naql). That is: you have described God, exalted is He, as having a partner. So it was said to Muhammad: ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, meaning your argument for that. This is rational, and reason rejects it, as has passed. Or it is transmitted, and that is revelation, and it too rejects it, for you will not find any book among the heavenly scriptures except that it contains His unity (tawhid) and His transcendence (tanzih) above having a partner. ﴿This﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿is the reminder of those with me﴾, meaning his community (ummah), ﴿and the reminder of those before me﴾, meaning the nations of the prophets before me. And it is in regard to the oneness of God and the negation of partners from Him. "Ma'iya" (with me) is read by Hafs. Since they did not refrain from their disbelief, He turned away from them and said: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know the truth﴾, that is, the Qur'an. It is in the accusative governed by ya'lamuna (they know). It is also read al-haqqu (the truth), meaning: it is the truth. ﴿So they are turning away﴾, on account of that, ﴿from consideration of what is incumbent upon them.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 21, verse 25:

﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him﴾: read as *nūḥī* (with *nūn*, "We reveal") by the Kūfī readers (the readers of the Kufan school), except Abū Bakr and Ḥammād. ﴿that there is no god except Me, so worship Me﴾: i.e., affirm My oneness (*waḥḥidūnī*). This verse confirms what precedes it of the verses of *tawḥīd* (affirmation of God's oneness).

It was revealed concerning the tribe of Khuza'ah, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." So He declared His essence free of that, then informed about them that they are servants, by His saying: ﴿Nay, they are honoured servants﴾. That is: rather, they are honoured servants, ennobled and brought near, and they are not offspring, since servitude (ʿubudiyyah) is incompatible with begetting (wilādah).

﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, i.e., with their speech. The lam has been put in place of the possessive (idafa). The meaning is: they follow His word, so their speech does not precede His speech, nor do they go ahead of His speech with their own words. ﴿And they act by His command﴾, i.e., just as their speech follows His speech, their action is likewise based on His command. They do not perform any action they have not been commanded to do.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 28:

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, i.e., their deeds, what they have put forward and what they have left behind. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾, i.e., for one with whom Allah the Exalted is pleased, or [the one who] says, "There is no god but Allah." ﴿And they are, out of fear of Him, apprehensive﴾, i.e., fearful.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 29:

﴿And whoever among them says﴾ — among the angels — ﴿"Indeed, I am a god besides Him"﴾ — besides Allah. The "innī" (إنِّي, "indeed I") is read as Madaniyy (Nafi' of Madina) and Abu 'Amr. ﴿Then that﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), meaning: then that speaker, his predicate (khabar) is ﴿We shall recompense him with Hell﴾, and this is the response (jawab) of the conditional (shart). ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾

the disbelievers, who placed divinity in other than its proper place. This is by way of supposition and illustration, given the certainty of their infallibility (ismah). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: the threat has been realized in Iblis, for he claimed divinity for himself and called to obedience to himself and worship of himself.

﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen﴾ (Makkī, the reader of the Meccan reading, reads it as "Have they not seen"), ﴿that the heavens and the earth were joined together﴾. That is, the heavens as a group and the earth as a group, which is why it does not say *kunna* (feminine plural). ﴿Ratqan﴾ (رَتْقًا) is used in the sense of the passive participle, meaning "they were sewn together" (*martūqatayn*). It is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), which is why it can stand in the place of *martūqatayn*. ﴿Then We parted them﴾ means "then We split them apart." *Fatq* (fatq, "parting") is separating two things, and *ratq* (ratq, "joining") is the opposite of *fatq*.

If it is asked, "When did they see them joined together, so that their acknowledgement of this could be established?", we answer: it is stated in the Qur'an, which is a miracle, so it takes the place of something seen and witnessed. Also, *ru'yah* (ru'yah, "seeing") here carries the meaning of *'ilm* (knowledge). The joining of the earth and the sky and their separation are both possible according to reason. So the specification of separation over joining requires a specifier, and that specifier is the Eternal, may His majesty be exalted.

Then it is said: the sky was joined to the earth with no space between them, and ﴿We parted them﴾ means "We separated them" (*faṣalnā baynahumā*) (p-402) by the air. It is also said that the heavens were a single stitched layer, and God Most High split them and made them seven heavens. Likewise, the earth was a single stitched layer, and He split it and made it seven earths. It is also said that the sky was joined and did not rain, and the earth was joined and did not grow plants, so He parted the sky with rain and the earth with plants.

﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ means "We created from water every living creature," as in His saying: ﴿And God created every creature from water﴾ [al-Nūr: 45]. Or it is as if We created it from water, because of its great need for it, its love for it, and its lack of patience without it, as in His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 37]. ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ means "will they not affirm what they witness?"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 31:

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾ — jibalan thawabita (firm mountains), from rasa, meaning it became firmly fixed when it settled. ﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾ — li'alla tadtariba bihim (lest it should convulse with them). So "la" (not) and the lam (the lam of purpose) were elided. The elision of "la" is permissible because there is no ambiguity, just as it is added for that same purpose in ﴿lest the People of the Book should know﴾ (li'alla ya'lama ahl al-kitab).

﴿And We placed in it broad paths﴾ — i.e., wide roads, plural of fajj, which is the wide road. It is put in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) qualifier of ﴿ways﴾ (subula), placed before it. If you ask: what is the difference between His saying, exalted is He, ﴿that you may follow therein broad paths﴾ [Nuh: 20] and this verse? I say: the first is to inform that He placed in it wide roads, and the second is to explain that when He created it, He created it with that attribute, so it is an explanation of what was left vague. Then ﴿that they may be guided﴾ (la'allahum yahtadun) — so that by them they may be guided to the intended lands.

And We made the sky a protected ceiling (﻿﴿وَجَعَلْنا السَماءَ سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا﴾). It is protected in its place from falling, as He said: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65]. Or it is protected by shooting stars from the devils, as He said: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ [al-Hijr: 17]. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿from its signs﴾, i.e., from the proofs in it such as the sun, the moon and the stars, ﴿are turning away﴾, not reflecting upon them so that they would believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 33:

﴿And it is He who created the night﴾ so that you may rest in it, ﴿and the day﴾ so that you may go about in it, ﴿and the sun﴾ so that it would be a lamp (sirāj) of the day, ﴿and the moon﴾ so that it would be a lamp of the night. ﴿Each﴾ — the tanwīn (nunation) in it is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the genitive noun that is added to (al-muḍāf ilayhi), i.e., "all of them" (kulluhum). The pronoun refers to the sun and the moon, and what is meant by them is the category of risers (al-ṭawāliʿ). It is put in the plural form used for rational beings (jamʿ al-ʿuqalāʾ) because it is described by their action, which is swimming (al-sibāḥa). ﴿In an orbit﴾ — it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the falak is the sky. However, the majority of scholars hold that the falak is a restrained (maknūf) current beneath the sky in which the sun, the moon and the stars move. ﴿Each﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿they swim﴾, i.e., they travel, meaning they revolve. The clause is in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the sun and the moon.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 34:

﴿And We did not grant to any human before you immortality﴾, the everlasting remaining (al-baqa' al-da'im). ﴿So if you die﴾ — with a kasra on the mim, according to Madani and Kufan readers except Abu Bakr — ﴿will they then be immortal?﴾ The first fa' is for coordinating one sentence with another (ʿatf jumla 'ala jumla), and the second is the response of the conditional (jaza' al-shart). They used to expect that he would die, so Allah negated for him the gloating over him by this, i.e., Allah has decreed that no human be made to remain forever in this world; so if you die, will these remain?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 35:

﴿Every soul shall taste death. And We test you⁠﴾ we try you and examine you. It is called "testing" (ibtila'), even though He knows what the doers of deeds will do before they come into existence, because it takes the form of examination. ﴿With evil﴾, that is, with poverty and harm, ﴿and good﴾, that is, wealth and benefit, ﴿as a trial﴾. Fitnah is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing "We test you," from a root other than its verb form. ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾, so We will recompense you according to what is found in you of patience and gratitude. And from Ibn Dhakwan, it is read "turja'un" (you are returned).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 36:

﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you only as a mockery﴾: "they take you" (yattakhidhunaka) — "only as a mockery" (ma yattakhidhunaka ﴿illa huzuwan﴾) is the second object (maf'ul thani) of yattakhidhunaka. It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl: the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him, so he laughed and said, "This is the prophet of the Banu 'Abd Manaf!" ﴿Is this the one who mentions﴾ — yaib, i.e., who criticizes — ﴿your gods?﴾ Mention (dhikr) can be with good or with its opposite. If the one mentioning is a friend, it is praise; if he is an enemy, it is blame. ﴿And they, at the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ — i.e., at the mention of God and what must be mentioned of Him in terms of His oneness — ﴿they are disbelievers﴾, who do not affirm it at all. So they are more deserving of being taken as a mockery by you, for you are in the right and they are in the wrong. It has also been said: "at the mention of the Most Merciful" means: (p-404) by what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, they are disbelievers, deniers. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), i.e., they take you as a mockery while they are in a state which is the root of mockery and derision, namely disbelief in God Most High. He repeated "they" (hum) for emphasis, or because the relative clause (silah) came between the subject and its predicate, so the subject was repeated.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 37:

﴿Man was created of haste.﴾ It has been interpreted as referring to the species (al-jins), and it is said that it was revealed when al-Nadr ibn al-Harith was asking for the punishment hastily. "Ajal" (haste) and "ajala" (hastiness) are both verbal nouns (masdar), and it means bringing a thing forward before its time. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the species, and that haste has been built into it, so it is as if it were created from haste, and because he frequently does it. The Arabs say of someone who is frequently generous, "He was created from generosity." So first He censured man for excessive haste and that he is naturally disposed to it, then He forbade him and rebuked him, as if He said: it is not strange of him that he should be hasty, for he is inclined to that by nature; it is his temperament and disposition, for it has been built into him. It has been said that "ajal" means clay in the language of Himyar, and their poet said:

"The nabk tree in the hard, smooth rock is its place of growth, and the palm tree grows between the water and the clay."

He was forbidden from haste although he is naturally disposed to it, just as He commanded him to suppress desire although He had placed it in him, because He gave him the strength by which he can suppress desire and abandon haste. And "min ajal" is a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning "hasty." ﴿I will show you My signs﴾, that is, My punishments, ﴿so do not ask Me to hasten them﴾ by bringing them. It is read with a ya' according to Ya'qub, and Sahl and Ayyash agreed with him in continuous recitation.

﴿They say, "When will this promise be fulfilled?"﴾ (It refers to) the coming of the punishment or the Resurrection. ﴿If you are truthful.﴾ It has been said that this is one of the two aspects of their haste.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 39:

﴿If only those who disbelieve knew the time when they will not be able to keep the Fire off their faces, nor off their backs, nor will they be helped.﴾ The answer to "law" (law, "if only") is omitted, and "ḥīn" (time) is the direct object of the verb "yaʿlam" (to know). That is: "If only they knew the time they are hastening for by their saying, 'When is this promise?'" It is a time in which the Fire will encompass them from behind and from in front, so they will not be able to repel it or ward it off from themselves, and they will find no helper to aid them. This is because they were in that state of disbelief, mockery and hastening; but their ignorance of it is what made it seem light to them.

Surah 21, verse 40. Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil):

﴿Nay, it will come upon them suddenly﴾ the Hour, ﴿and will confound them﴾ that is, bewilder them. Meaning: they cannot avert it; rather it will take them by surprise and overpower them. ﴿So they will not be able to repel it﴾ so they will have no power to ward it off, ﴿nor will they be given respite﴾ they will not be granted a reprieve.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 41:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but there befell﴾ — "fa-haqa" (befell, encompassed) means it came down upon, ﴿those among them who scoffed﴾ the requital of ﴿what they used to mock at﴾. He (al-Nasafi) consoles the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning their mockery of him, by informing him that in the prophets there is for him an exemplar (uswah), and that what they do to him will befall them, just as there befell those who mocked the prophets what they had done.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 42:

﴿Say: Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?﴾ (yaḥfaẓukum) guards you, ﴿from the Most Merciful﴾, that is, from His punishment, should it come upon you by night or by day. ﴿Rather, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, that is, rather, they turn away from His remembrance and do not bring it to their minds, let alone fear His might. ﴿Until, when they are granted protection from Him, they know who the one who protects is, and become fit to be asked about Him.﴾ The meaning is: He commanded His Messenger to ask them about the one who protects, then explained that they are not fit for that because of their turning away from the remembrance of the One who protects them. Then He turned away from that with His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 43:

﴿Or do they have gods that protect them from Us?﴾ This is because "am" (or) carries the meaning of "bal" (rather), so it says: "Do they have gods that protect them from the punishment, exceeding Our protection and preservation?" Then he resumed with His saying: ﴿They are unable to help themselves, nor will they be accompanied by Us (with aid).﴾ Thus He made clear that one who is not able to help himself or to defend himself, and is not accompanied by Allah with victory and support, how could he protect and help others?

Then he said: (p-406)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 44:

﴿Nay, We gave these people and their fathers enjoyment until a long life passed over them.﴾ Meaning: what they have of protection and safekeeping comes only from Us, not from any preventer who could stop them from destroying us. We did not keep them and their past fathers safe except as a means of giving them enjoyment of the life of this world and granting them respite, just as We gave enjoyment to other unbelievers and granted them respite, until the term grew long for them, so their hearts hardened and they supposed that they would remain forever in that state. This is a false hope. ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ Meaning: We diminish the land of unbelief and cut away its outlying parts by giving the Muslims power over it, making them victorious over its people, and turning it into a land of Islam. The mention of "We come" (na'ti) indicates that God brings this about through the hands of the Muslims, and that their armies used to raid the land of the polytheists and came to it prevailing over it, having reduced it from its outlying parts. ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ Do the unbelievers of Makkah get defeated after We have reduced the outlying parts of their land? Meaning: it is not so; rather, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions will overcome them by Our help.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 45:

﴿Say, "I only warn you by the revelation."﴾ I warn you of the punishment by means of the Qur'an. ﴿But the deaf do not hear the call﴾ — read with the letter yā' open and the letter mīm open, and with the ḍamma on the ṣumm (ṣumm being the subject), and "﴿lā tusmiʿu al-ṣumma﴾" (you do not make the deaf hear) is the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī), addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿when they are warned﴾ — they are made afraid. The definite article in al-ṣumm is for previous reference (lil-ʿahd), and it points to these warned people. The original construction would be "and they do not hear when they are warned," so the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate their deafness and their stopping up their ears when they are warned.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 46:**

﴿And if a breath (nafḥa) of your Lord's punishment should touch them﴾: *dufʿa yasīra*, a slight push, a small instance. ﴿of your Lord's punishment﴾: *ṣifa* (attribute, qualifier) *li-nafḥa*, a qualifier of *nafḥa*. ﴿they will surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ Meaning: if even the slightest part of this (punishment) with which they are warned were to touch them, they would be humbled, call down woe upon themselves, and acknowledge that they had wronged themselves, since they had remained deaf and turned away. The expression is intensified in mentioning *mass* (touch) and *nafḥa* (breath), because *nafḥ* indicates a small amount. It is said: *nafaḥahu bi-ʿaṭiyya*, meaning he gave him a gift, *radakhahu bihā*, meaning he presented him with it. Although its form (*bināʾuhā*) is for the single occurrence (*li-l-marra*). (p-407)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 47:

﴿And We shall set up the scales (al-mawazin)﴾ The plural of mizan (scale), which is that by which a thing is weighed so that its quantity is known. It is narrated from al-Hasan that it is a scale having two pans and a tongue (lisan). The plural mawazin was used to magnify its status, as in His saying ﴿O messengers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]. The weighing is of the records of deeds, according to one opinion. ﴿Justice (al-qist)﴾: the scales are described as "justice," which means fairness (al-adl), as an intensification, as if they themselves were justice; or it is by omission of a modifier, meaning possessors of justice. ﴿For the Day of Resurrection﴾: for the people of the Day of Resurrection, i.e., for their sake. ﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything﴾: in the sense of injustice. ﴿Even if it be the weight of a mustard seed (mithqal habbah)﴾: even if the thing is the weight of a grain (habbah). 

﴿Mithqal⁠﴾ with the nominative (marfu') is read by the people of Medina (Madani), and likewise in Luqman, taking kana as the complete (tammah) verb. ﴿Of a mustard seed (min khardal)﴾ is an adjective of habbah. ﴿We will bring it forth (atayna biha)﴾: we will bring it into presence. The pronoun referring to mithqal is feminine because it is annexed to habbah, as in their saying "some of his fingers went (dhahabat ba'du asabi'ihi)." ﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners (hasibin)﴾: knowing and guarding. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because whoever guards something counts it and knows it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 48:

﴿And We certainly gave Musa and Harun the Criterion (al-Furqan), and a light (diya') and a reminder (dhikr)﴾ It is said: these three are the Torah. So it is al-Furqan, a distinguishing between the truth and falsehood; and a light (diya'), by which one is illuminated and through which one reaches the path of salvation; and a reminder (dhikr), that is, an honour (sharaf), or admonition and alerting (wa'z wa tanbih), or a mention of what people need in the matters of their religion. The waw (and) has entered upon the attributes, as in His saying ﴿and a chief, and chaste, and a prophet﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39]. You say: "I passed by Zayd the generous, the learned, and the righteous." And since the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) benefited from this, He specified them with His saying ﴿for the God-fearing﴾.

The place of ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who) may be in the genitive as a qualifying adjective (sifa), or in the accusative by way of praise (madh), or in the nominative with that as its implied predicate. ﴿Yakhshawna rabbahum﴾ (they fear their Lord) means: ﴿yakhafunahu﴾ (they fear Him). ﴿Bil-ghayb﴾ (in secret) is a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: they fear Him in privacy, when no one is watching. ﴿Wa hum min al-sa'a﴾ (and they are of the Hour) means of the Resurrection (al-qiyamah) and its terrors, ﴿mushfiquna﴾ (fearful), meaning: fearing (kha'ifun).

And this [Qur'an] is a blessed reminder (dhikr mubarak), abundant in good and plentiful in benefit, which We have sent down [upon Muhammad (ﷺ)]. ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾ This is a question of rebuke, meaning: Will you deny that it is sent down from Allah?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 51:

﴿And We certainly gave Ibrahim his rushd﴾ — his guidance (hudahu) — ﴿from before﴾ — from before the time of Musa and Harun, or from before Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And We were of him﴾ — of Ibrahim, or of his rushd — ﴿knowing﴾, i.e., We knew that he was worthy of what We had given him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 52:

﴿When⁠﴾ may be connected either with "We gave" (ātaynā) or with "his right guidance." ﴿He said to his father and his people: "What are these images (tamāthīl) to which you are devoted?"﴾ That is, the idols (al-aṣnām) fashioned in the forms of beasts, birds and humans. In this there is a feigned ignorance on his part toward them, in order to belittle their gods, although he knew how greatly they revered them. ﴿to which you are devoted⁠﴾ means: remaining constantly in their worship. So when they were unable to produce proof for that,
They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them," so we followed them.

Ibrahim said: "Indeed you and your fathers have been in clear error." He meant that the imitators and those who are imitated are enrolled in a thread of manifest error that is not hidden from any person of intellect. He emphasized with "antum" (you) so that the conjunction would be valid, because coordinating (ʿatf) upon the pronoun within the verb (the pronoun in kuntum) is, in effect, part of the verb and is therefore impermissible.

﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth" (bi'l-jidd, in earnest) ﴿or are you one of the jesters?"﴾ That is: are you serious in what you say, or are you playing? They said this in astonishment at his denouncing them and in disbelief that what they were upon could be misguidance.

Then he turned away from them, informing that he was in earnest about what he said, not a player (in jest), affirming the lordship of the All-Knowing King and the createdness of the idols, by his saying ﴿"Nay, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them"﴾ — that is, the statues. So how can the created be worshipped and the Creator be abandoned? ﴿"And I am of those who bear witness to that"﴾ — that is, to the aforementioned monotheism ﴿"of the witnesses"﴾. (p. 409)

"And by Allah" — its origin is "wa-Allahi," and in the particle "ta" there is a sense of wonder at how the scheming against them was made easy at his hand, despite its difficulty and near impossibility, given the strength of Nimrod's authority. ﴿I will surely scheme against your idols﴾ — I will surely break them ﴿after you have turned away, retreating﴾ — after your departure from them to your festival. He said that secretly, away from his people, but one man heard him, so he alluded to it with his words "Indeed, I am sick" — meaning: I will become sick — so that he might remain behind, and [Abraham] returned to the house of the idols.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 58:

﴿So he made them into fragments﴾: pieces, from al-jadhdh (jadhdh is cutting). Judhadhan (جُذاذًا) is the plural of judhadha (جُذاذَةٍ), like zujaja (زُجاجَةٍ) and zujaj (زُجاجٍ). Judhadhan (جِذاذًا) with a kasra is read by ʿAli, as the plural of jadhidh (جَذِيذٍ), meaning majdhudh (مَجْذُوذٍ, "cut"), like khafif (خَفِيفٍ) and khaf (خافٍ). ﴿Except a great one among them﴾: for the idols, or for the disbelievers. That is, he broke them all with an axe in his hand, except the great one, on whose neck he hung the axe. ﴿So that they might return to it﴾: to the great one, ﴿and ask it about the one who broke them﴾, so that its inability would become clear to them. Or to Ibrahim, so that he could argue against them. Or to Allah, when they saw the inability of their gods.

ِ﴿They said﴾, that is, the disbelievers, when they returned from their festival and saw that: ﴿Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is surely among the wrongdoers﴾, that is: whoever did this smashing is indeed greatly wrongful, for his audacity toward the gods, which they regarded as true objects of reverence and veneration.

﴿They said: "We heard a youth mention them, who is called Ibrahim."﴾ The two clauses are both descriptions of "a youth" (fata). However, the first, "yadhkuruhum" (i.e., he speaks ill of them, criticizes them), is necessary for "sami'a" (heard), because you do not say "I heard Zayd" and then stop until you mention something of what is heard. This differs from the second clause. The nominative case of ﴿Ibrahim﴾ is because it is the subject (fa'il) of ﴿yuqalu﴾ (is called). So what is meant is the name, not the named one; that is, the one to whom this name is said.

﴿They said﴾, that is, Nimrod and the nobles of his people: ﴿Bring him﴾, bring Ibrahim ﴿before the eyes of the people﴾, the phrase being in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning "in plain view and witnessed," that is, in their sight and presence, ﴿so that they may bear witness﴾ against him by what they heard from him or by what he did. It is as though they disliked punishing him without clear proof, or [the meaning is] that they may witness our punishment of him.

**Verses 62–63.** When they had brought him, ﴿They said, "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ (62) ﴿He said, "Rather, this one, their chief, did it. So ask them, if they can speak."﴾

**62–63 –** When they had brought him, ﴿They said, "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ ﴿He said﴾ Ibrahim, ﴿"Rather, their chief did it"﴾. Al-Kisa'i (al-Kisa'i) reported that he would pause (waqf) on the word ﴿فَعَلَهُ﴾ (fa'alahu, "he did it"), meaning: "Whoever did it did it." In this reading there is an elision of the agent (hadhf al-fa'il), and this is not permissible. It is possible, however, that the agent refers back to the youth mentioned in His words, ﴿"We heard a youth mention them"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 60], and that the reference to Ibrahim in "O Ibrahim" is a separate matter. Then he said, ﴿"their chief, this one"﴾, where ﴿كَبِيرُهم﴾ (kabiruhum, "their chief") is a subject (mubtada') and ﴿هَذا﴾ (hadha, "this") is a predicate (khabar). Most readers do not pause here. The agent is ﴿كَبِيرُهم﴾, and ﴿هَذا﴾ is either a descriptive qualifier (sifah) or an apposition (badal).

He attributed the act to their chief, and his intention was to affirm it for himself and establish it for himself, by way of allusion (ta'ridh), as a rebuke to them and a binding of the proof upon them. This is because, if they looked at the matter correctly, they would know the helplessness of their chief and that he is not fit to be a god. An analogy: suppose your companion, seeing a book you had written in a fine, elegant hand, said, "Did you write this, while your companion is illiterate?" and you replied, "Rather, you wrote it." Your purpose in this answer would be to affirm it to him while mocking him, not to deny it of yourself and affirm it of the illiterate one, because affirming it to the powerless one of the two of you, when the matter lies between you two, is mockery of him and affirmation of the capable one.

It is also possible to say that those idols angered him when he saw them lined up, and the anger of their chief was greater because of what he saw of their excessive veneration of him. So he ascribed the act to him, because an act is ascribed both to the one who carries it out and to the one who moves to it. It is also possible that this is a report of what leads to the supposition of their creed: as if he said to them, "What do you find so strange about their chief doing this? For whoever is worshipped and called a god ought to be able to do this." It is related that he said, "He was angry that these small ones should be worshipped alongside him, when he is greater than them, so he smashed them."

Alternatively, the clause is linked to a condition that does not occur, namely the idols' speech. Then it is a negation of what is reported about them, meaning: "Rather, their chief did it, if they can speak." His words ﴿فاسْألُوهُمْ﴾ (fas'aluhum, "so ask them") are a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). It has been said that he alluded to himself through the chief. He attributed himself to them only because they were together in attendance.

﴿So ask them﴾ about their condition, ﴿if they can speak﴾, while you know their inability to do that.

**Verses 62–63.** When they had brought him, ﴿They said, "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ (62) ﴿He said, "Rather, this one, their chief, did it. So ask them, if they can speak."﴾

**62–63 –** When they had brought him, ﴿They said, "Is it you who did this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ ﴿He said﴾ Ibrahim, ﴿"Rather, their chief did it"﴾. Al-Kisa'i (al-Kisa'i) reported that he would pause (waqf) on the word ﴿فَعَلَهُ﴾ (fa'alahu, "he did it"), meaning: "Whoever did it did it." In this reading there is an elision of the agent (hadhf al-fa'il), and this is not permissible. It is possible, however, that the agent refers back to the youth mentioned in His words, ﴿"We heard a youth mention them"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 60], and that the reference to Ibrahim in "O Ibrahim" is a separate matter. Then he said, ﴿"their chief, this one"﴾, where ﴿كَبِيرُهم﴾ (kabiruhum, "their chief") is a subject (mubtada') and ﴿هَذا﴾ (hadha, "this") is a predicate (khabar). Most readers do not pause here. The agent is ﴿كَبِيرُهم﴾, and ﴿هَذا﴾ is either a descriptive qualifier (sifah) or an apposition (badal).

He attributed the act to their chief, and his intention was to affirm it for himself and establish it for himself, by way of allusion (ta'ridh), as a rebuke to them and a binding of the proof upon them. This is because, if they looked at the matter correctly, they would know the helplessness of their chief and that he is not fit to be a god. An analogy: suppose your companion, seeing a book you had written in a fine, elegant hand, said, "Did you write this, while your companion is illiterate?" and you replied, "Rather, you wrote it." Your purpose in this answer would be to affirm it to him while mocking him, not to deny it of yourself and affirm it of the illiterate one, because affirming it to the powerless one of the two of you, when the matter lies between you two, is mockery of him and affirmation of the capable one.

It is also possible to say that those idols angered him when he saw them lined up, and the anger of their chief was greater because of what he saw of their excessive veneration of him. So he ascribed the act to him, because an act is ascribed both to the one who carries it out and to the one who moves to it. It is also possible that this is a report of what leads to the supposition of their creed: as if he said to them, "What do you find so strange about their chief doing this? For whoever is worshipped and called a god ought to be able to do this." It is related that he said, "He was angry that these small ones should be worshipped alongside him, when he is greater than them, so he smashed them."

Alternatively, the clause is linked to a condition that does not occur, namely the idols' speech. Then it is a negation of what is reported about them, meaning: "Rather, their chief did it, if they can speak." His words ﴿فاسْألُوهُمْ﴾ (fas'aluhum, "so ask them") are a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). It has been said that he alluded to himself through the chief. He attributed himself to them only because they were together in attendance.

﴿So ask them﴾ about their condition, ﴿if they can speak﴾, while you know their inability to do that.

﴿So they returned to themselves﴾ — that is, they returned to their intellects and reflected with their hearts, once his (Abraham's) opposition had struck them. ﴿So they said: "Indeed you yourselves are the wrongdoers"﴾ — in truth, by worshipping that which does not speak, not the one whom you wronged when you said: ﴿"Who has done this to our gods? Indeed he is among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya: 59]. For how can one who cannot ward off the axe from his own head ward off harm from his worshippers?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 65:

﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads.﴾ The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: God, exalted is He, made the truth flow on their tongues in the first statement; then wretchedness overtook them. That is, they were returned to disbelief after they had acknowledged against themselves their wrongdoing. It is said: "nakastuhu" (I overturned it) means I turned it over, so I made its lower part its upper part. That is, they stood upright when they returned to themselves and brought forth sound reasoning, then they turned away from that state and took to disputation with falsehood and obstinacy, and they said: ﴿Indeed you know that these do not speak.﴾ So how do you command us to ask them? The clause (jumlah) took the place of the two objects of "alimta" (you knew). The meaning is: You surely know their inability to speak, so how should we ask them?

"He said," arguing against them: "Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?" ﴿Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?﴾ The word "شَيْئًا" (shay'an, "at all") is in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "benefit" (naf'an). ﴿and cannot harm you﴾ if you do not worship it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 67:

﴿Fie upon you, and upon what you worship besides Allah! Have you no sense?﴾ "Uff" (أُفٍّ) is a sound which, when uttered, makes it known that the one uttering it is impatient and annoyed. What annoyed him (Ibrahim) was what he saw of their persistence in worshipping them after the excuse had been cut off from them and after the truth had become clear, so he expressed his impatience at them. The lam (ل) is for specifying the object of the exclamation, i.e., "for you and for your gods is this exclamation." "Uffin" (أُفٍّ) is read by Madani and Hafs; "Uff" (أُفَّ) is read by Makki and Shami; and "Uffi" (أُفِّ) by the rest. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, that one with this description cannot be a god. So when the proof became binding upon them and they were unable to answer...

﴿They said, "Burn him"⁠﴾ with fire, because it is the most terrifying and dreadful of punishments, ﴿"and support your gods"⁠﴾ by avenging yourselves on him, ﴿"if you are going to act."⁠﴾ That is: if you are going to be supporters of your gods with a strong support, then choose for him the most terrifying of punishments, which is burning with fire; otherwise you have neglected their support. (p-412) The one who suggested burning him was Nimrod, or a man from the Kurds of Persia. It was said that when they resolved to burn him, they imprisoned him, then built a structure at Kuthā and gathered for a month various kinds of wood, then they lit a great fire, so that the birds nearly burned in the air from its heat. Then they placed him in the catapult, bound and shackled, and threw him into it, while he was saying, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." Gabriel said to him, "Do you have any need?" He said, "As for you, no." He said, "Then ask your Lord." He said, "My knowledge of my condition is sufficient for me instead of asking." The fire burned nothing but his bonds. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was saved only by his saying, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 69:

﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety﴾ meaning: possessing coolness and safety. This is intensified in expression, as though its very essence were coolness and safety. ﴿upon Ibrahim﴾. He intended: "Be cool, so that Ibrahim is safe from you." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that had He not said that, it would have destroyed him with its coolness. The meaning is: Allah the Exalted removed from it the nature with which He had created it, of heat and burning, and left it with its light and brightness as it was. And He is Powerful over all things.

[Qur'anic quotation] "And they intended a plot against him" — namely, burning him. [Qur'anic quotation] "So We made them the greatest losers."

Then gnats (baʿūḍ, the plural of baʿūḍa, a tiny biting insect) were sent upon Nimrod (Namrud) and his people. They ate their flesh and drank their blood, and a single gnat entered the brain of Nimrod and destroyed him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 71:

﴿And We delivered him﴾, that is, Ibrahim, ﴿and Lut﴾, the son of his brother Haran, ﴿from the land of Iraq to the land which We had blessed for all the worlds﴾. That is: the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Its blessing lies in the fact that most of the prophets came from it, so their religious traces spread throughout the worlds. It is a fertile land in which the life of both the rich and the poor is pleasant. It was also said: there is no sweet water in the land except that its source springs from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is narrated that he (Ibrahim) settled in Filastin, and Lut in al-Mu'tafikah, and between them was a distance of one day and one night's journey. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there will be a migration after a migration, and the best of people will be at the place of migration of Ibrahim."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 72:

﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift (nafilah)﴾ It is said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-'afiyah, not derived from the preceding verb; that is, "We bestowed upon him a bestowal." And it is said that nafilah means a son's son (grandson). He had asked for a son and was given one, and Jacob was given as a nafilah, that is, as an increase and a favour without his asking. And it (nafilah) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of Jacob. ﴿And all﴾ that is, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and it is the first object (al-maf'ul al-awwal) of His saying ﴿We made﴾, and the second is ﴿righteous﴾ in religion and prophethood.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 73:**

﴿And We made them leaders﴾ who are followed in religion, ﴿guiding﴾ people ﴿by Our command﴾, by Our revelation. ﴿And We inspired them to do good deeds﴾, which encompass all righteous actions. The original form is that the good deeds be done, then "فِعْلًا الخَيْراتِ" (fi'lan al-khayrat), with the verbal noun (fi'l) governing "al-khayrat" as its object. Likewise is His saying ﴿and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat﴾. The original is "wa-iqamat al-salat" (the establishment of the prayer), but the genitive-possessed noun (al-mudaf) was made a substitute for the feminine ending "ha'" (the taa marbuta), so that the possessed noun (al-mudaf ilayhi, "the noun in the genitive that follows") took its place. ﴿And they were worshippers of Us﴾, not of idols. So you, O assembly of the Arabs, are the descendants of Abraham, so follow him in that.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 74:**

﴿And Lot⁠﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb that is explained by ﴿We gave him judgment⁠﴾: ḥukm (judgment), meaning ḥikmah (wisdom), which is what one must do in terms of action; or a decisive ruling between disputants; or prophethood. ﴿And knowledge⁠﴾: fiqh (jurisprudence). ﴿And We rescued him from the town⁠﴾: from its people, and it is Sodom, ﴿which used to commit abominations⁠﴾: sodomy (al-lūṭah), flatulence (al-ḍirāṭah), and throwing pebbles at passers-by (ḥadhf al-māarra bil-ḥaṣā), and others. ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient⁠﴾: going out of obedience to God.

"And We admitted him into Our mercy" — into the people of Our mercy, or into Paradise. "Indeed he was among the righteous" — that is, as a reward for him for his righteousness, just as We destroyed his people as a punishment for their corruption.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 76:**

﴿And Noah﴾, i.e., remember Noah, ﴿when he called out﴾, i.e., he supplicated against his people for their destruction, ﴿before﴾, before these mentioned ones. ﴿So We responded to him﴾, i.e., to his supplication (p-414) ﴿and saved him and his family﴾, i.e., the believers among his children and his people, ﴿from the great distress﴾, i.e., from the flood and the denial of the people of rebellion.

"And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs." (We protected him from them, i.e., from their harm.) "Indeed they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all," (the young and the old of them, their males and their females).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 78:**

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman﴾ i.e., mention them both. ﴿When﴾ is a substitute (badal) for them both: ﴿they were judging concerning the tilth﴾, that is, the field of crops or the vineyard, ﴿when﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) governed by ﴿they were judging﴾. ﴿The flocks of the people grazed in it﴾, that is, entered it, ﴿by night﴾, and so they ate it and ruined it. Al-nafsh (dispersal) is the scattering of sheep at night without a shepherd. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, meaning: He, them, and the litigants who came before them. That is, it was by Our knowledge and in Our sight that this took place.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 79:

﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Solomon﴾, that is, the judgment or the ruling. In this there is evidence that the correct judgment was with Solomon, may the blessings of God be upon him. The story is that sheep grazed on a field and damaged it at night, without a shepherd, so the two parties brought the dispute to David, and he ruled that the sheep be given to the owners of the field. The value of the two was equal, that is, the value of the sheep was equal to the amount of the damage to the field. Solomon, who was eleven years old, said: "Other than this is more gentle to both parties." He insisted that David rule otherwise, so David said: "What do you think?" Solomon said: "I think the sheep should be handed over to the owners of the field, so that they may benefit from their milk, their young and their wool, and the field should be handed over to the owner of the sheep until he repairs the field and it returns to the condition it was in on the day it was damaged. Then they should exchange back." David said: "The judgment is what you have judged," and he enforced the ruling accordingly. This was by ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) on the part of both of them. This was in their sharia (divine law). As for our sharia, Abu Hanifa and his companions, may God have mercy on him, hold that there is no liability, whether by night or by day, unless the animal has a driver or a leader with it. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, liability is required at night. Al-Jassas said: "They were liable only because they had released the animals, and the liability was abrogated (naskh) by his words, peace and blessings be upon him: 'The animal's injury is unrequited' (al-'ajma' jubar)." (p-415) Mujahid said: "This was a settlement (sulh), and what David did was a judgment, and settlement is better." ﴿And to each﴾ of David and Solomon, ﴿We gave judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 74], meaning prophethood, ﴿and knowledge﴾, meaning understanding of the implications of the judgment. ﴿And We subjected﴾, meaning We made subservient and tractable, ﴿the mountains to glorify [God] along with David﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of "glorifying," or it is a new sentence, as if someone asked: "How did He subject them?" and the answer was: "They glorify [God]." ﴿And the birds﴾ is coordinated with the mountains, or it is an object with "along with" (maf'ul ma'ahu). The mountains are mentioned before the birds because their subjection and their glorification are more wondrous, more remarkable, and more included in the miraculous, since they are inanimate. It is narrated that he would pass by the mountains glorifying God while they responded to him. It is also said that they would travel with him wherever he went. ﴿And We were the ones who did [this]﴾ with the prophets, the like of that, even if it seems wondrous to you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 80:

﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you﴾, i.e., the craft of making *al-labus* (coats of mail) and *al-duruʿ* (armor). *Al-labus*: clothing; and what is meant is the coat of mail (*al-dirʿ*). ﴿So that it may protect you﴾ — Ibn ʿAmir (al-Shami) and Hafs read it as *li-tuhsinakum* with the *ta* (the verb is feminine, referring to the craft); Abu Bakr and Hammad read it with *nun* (*li-nuhsinakum*), meaning God, Mighty and Majestic is He; and the rest read it with *ya* (*li-yuhsinakum*), meaning the coat of mail, or God, Mighty and Majestic is He. ﴿From your violence﴾ — from the fighting of your enemy. ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ — an interrogative with the meaning of a command, i.e., so give thanks to God for that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 81:

﴿And to Sulayman (We subjected) the wind﴾, i.e., We made the wind subservient to him, ﴿violently blowing﴾, which is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., of strong blowing. It is described elsewhere as ﴿gentle﴾, because it runs by his choice; so at one time it was gentle and at another time violently blowing, according to the dictates of his will in its blowing. ﴿It ran by his command﴾, by the command of Sulayman, ﴿to the land which We had blessed﴾ with abundance of rivers, trees and fruits. What is meant is al-Sham (Greater Syria), where his dwelling was, and the wind would carry him to it from the various regions of the earth. ﴿And We have been, of all things, Knowing﴾, for Our knowledge encompasses everything, so all things proceed in accordance with what Our knowledge requires. (p-416)

and of the devils, [We subjected] those who dove for him (لَهُ) in the seas by His command, to extract pearls and what is in them; ﴿and they did work other than that﴾, i.e., other than diving, which was the building of prayer-niches (مَحارِيب), statues (تَماثِيل), palaces (قُصُور), cooking-pots (قُدُور) and large basins (جِفان); ﴿and We were Guardians over them﴾, lest they swerve from His command, or alter [it], or corruption be found among them in what they were subjected to.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 83:**

﴿And Ayyub﴾, meaning: mention Ayyub, ﴿when he called out to his Lord, "Indeed, harm has touched me"﴾, meaning: he called upon Him, saying that harm had touched him. ﴿Harm﴾ (ḍarr) with a fatḥah means harm in all things, and with a ḍammah means harm to oneself, such as from sickness or emaciation. ﴿And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾. He was most gentle in his supplication, for he mentioned himself with that which calls for mercy, and he mentioned his Lord with the utmost of mercy, and did not state the request explicitly. It is as if he said: You are worthy to show mercy, and Ayyub is worthy to be shown mercy, so have mercy upon him and remove from him the affliction that has touched him. It is narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he reported of his weakness when he was unable to rise for prayer, and he did not complain. And how could one complain who was told, ﴿Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant﴾ [Sad: 44]? It has been said that he only complained to Him out of delight in intimate communion, not out of distress caused by complaining; and complaining to Him is the utmost of nearness, just as complaining about Him is the utmost of distance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 84:

﴿So We answered him﴾ — We answered his supplication. ﴿And We removed what was upon him of affliction﴾ — We removed his harm, as a favour bestowed upon him. ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾

It is related that Ayyub (peace be upon him) was a Roman, of the descendants of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim (peace be upon him). He had seven sons and seven daughters, three thousand camels, seven thousand sheep, and five hundred plough-oxen (faddan) followed by five hundred servants, each servant having a wife and a child, and palm trees. Then Allah the Exalted tested him with the loss of his children and his wealth, and with an illness in his body, for eighteen years, or thirteen years, or three years. (p-417) One day his wife said to him, "If only you would call upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." He said, "How long was the period of ease?" She said, "Eighty years." He said, "I am ashamed before Allah to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease." Then, when Allah removed his affliction, He restored his children to him in their very persons, and gave him the like of them with them. ﴿A mercy from Us﴾ — this is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). ﴿And a reminder for the worshippers﴾ — that is, a mercy to Ayyub and a reminder to others among the worshippers, so that they may endure with patience as he did, and be rewarded with his reward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 85:

﴿And Isma'il﴾ (the son of Ibrahim), ﴿and Idris﴾ (the son of Shith, son of Adam), ﴿and Dhul-Kifl﴾: i.e., mention them. He is Ilyas, or Zakariyya, or Yusha' ibn Nun, and he was named so because he had a share (ḥaẓẓ) from Allah; al-kifl means a share (ḥaẓẓ). ﴿Each of them was among the patient ones﴾: i.e., all those mentioned were described as being patient.

["And We admitted them into Our mercy"] — (that is) into Our prophethood, or into the blessing in the Hereafter. ["Indeed they were among the righteous"] — i.e., among those whose righteousness is not clouded by the turbidity of corruption.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 87:

﴿And Dhu'l-Nun﴾ means: remember the companion of the fish. Al-Nun is the fish (al-hut), and he is thus annexed to it. ﴿When he went off in anger﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: angry at (muraghiman li-qawmihi), that is, defying his people. The meaning of his anger at his people is that he angered them by leaving them, because they feared the descent of punishment upon them at that time. It is narrated that he became fed up with his people because of the long time he admonished them, yet they did not heed and persisted in their disbelief. So he defied them, and he thought that this was permissible, since he did it only out of zeal for God and hatred of disbelief and its people. It was incumbent upon him to be patient and to await permission from God, Exalted, regarding emigrating from them, but he was tested with the belly of the fish. ﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him﴾ (lan naqdira, we would not constrict, ʿalayhi, upon him). It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he entered upon Muʿawiyah one day and said: "The waves of the Qur'an struck me last night, and I drowned in them, and I found no escape for myself except through you." He said: "And what is it, O Muʿawiyah?" So he recited the verse. Muʿawiyah said: "Does the Prophet of Allah think that He would not have power over him?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "This is from qadar (decree), not from qudrah (power)."

﴿So he called out in the darknesses﴾ means: in the intense, thick darkness in the belly of the fish, like His saying: ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], or the darkness of the night, the sea, and the belly of the fish. (p-418) ﴿That﴾ means: that ﴿there is no god but You﴾, or it carries the sense of "i.e.": ﴿Glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ against myself, in my leaving my people before You gave me permission. In a hadith: "No distressed person supplicates with this supplication except that it is answered for him." It is narrated from al-Hasan: Allah did not save him except through his confession of wrongdoing against himself.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 88:

﴿So We answered him and delivered him from the distress﴾ — the distress of the slip (zallah), of loneliness (wahshah), and of solitude (wahdah). ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾ — when they call upon Us and seek help from Us. "Nunji" is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (al-Shāmī) and Abū Bakr [ʿĀṣim] with the assimilation of the nūn into the jīm, according to some, because the nūn is not assimilated into the jīm. It was also said that its underlying form is: nujjiya al-nijāʾu al-muʾminīna (the deliverance delivered the believers), so the yāʾ was made sukūn for lightness, the verb was ascribed to the verbal noun (maṣdar), and al-muʾminīn was put in the accusative by al-nijāʾ. But in this there is the placing of the verbal noun in the position of the subject (nāʾib al-fāʿil) while the object is present, and this is not permissible; and in it there is the sukūn of the yāʾ, whose proper place is in cases of necessity (ḍarūrāt). It was also said that its original form is nunajjī, from al-tanjiyah (deliverance), and the second nūn was deleted because of the gathering of two nūns, just as one of the two tāʾs was deleted in ﴿tanazzalu al-malāʾikah﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 89:

﴿And Zechariah, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ He asked his Lord to grant him a child who would inherit from him, and not to leave him alone, without an heir. Then he referred his matter to Allah, submitting, and said: ﴿And You are the best of inheritors.﴾ That is: if You do not grant me one who will inherit from me, I will not be concerned, for You are the best of inheritors, that is, the One who remains.

ﷺ

﴿So We answered him and granted him Yahya﴾ as a child, ﴿and We made his wife fit for him﴾, meaning We made her fit for bearing children after she had been barren, or made her good-natured, whereas she had had a bad disposition. ﴿Indeed they﴾, that is, the prophets mentioned, ﴿used to hasten to good deeds﴾. That is: they merited having their supplications answered only because they hurried to the doors of good and were swift in attaining them. (p-419) ﴿And they called upon Us in hope and fear﴾. That is, in desire and in dread, like His saying ﴿fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. Both are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: out of eagerness for Us and awe of Us. ﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾, humble and fearful.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 91:

﴿And she who﴾, that is: mention her who ﴿guarded her chastity﴾, keeping it from both the lawful and the unlawful. ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾. We caused the spirit of the Messiah to enter her, or We commanded Jibril (Gabriel), and he breathed into the collar of her shift (dir', a long garment), and by that breath We brought about Isa (Jesus) in her womb. The attribution of the Spirit to Him, exalted is He, is to honour Isa, peace be upon him. ﴿And We made her and her son a sign﴾, the second object, ﴿for the worlds﴾.
